confidence_note: Checked against the book text (chapter 4 'One Thousand and One Days' and chapter 13). The old reference text built the story on 'antifragile', a concept from Taleb's later book Antifragile (2012), not The Black Swan; it is dropped. The story is rebuilt on the book's own turkey problem and barbell strategy. Percentages (85-90 / 10-15) are Taleb's illustration for money, not a rule for life.
facts: In The Black Swan, Taleb borrows a problem from the philosopher Bertrand Russell (who used a chicken) and tells it with a turkey that is fed every day.
Every feeding firms up the turkey's belief that humans are looking after its interests.
On the afternoon of the Wednesday before Thanksgiving it is killed. Its feeling of safety was at its highest when the risk was at its highest.
The chart in the book is titled 'One thousand and one days of history': a thousand days of data say nothing about day 1,001.

Taleb's answer as a former trader is the barbell: instead of 'medium risk', put about 85 to 90 percent of money in extremely safe instruments such as Treasury bills and 10 to 15 percent in extremely speculative bets.
That way no Black Swan can push you below your floor, while the small speculative part stays open to big surprises.

He separates positive and negative Black Swan activities: in film, some publishing, scientific research and venture capital you lose small to win big; in banking, lending or catastrophe insurance surprises mostly hurt.
He quotes screenwriter William Goldman on film sales: 'Nobody knows anything.'
His summary: invest in preparedness, not in prediction.
scene_details: a turkey fed every day for a thousand days
Treasury bills on one end, speculative bets on the other
tension: The longer things go well, the safer the turkey feels, right up to the day they do not.
opening_idea: Start with the turkey and the daily feeding, without naming the day yet.

lessons.idea: Split your exposure: make the downside you cannot survive very safe, and take small, cheap bets where a surprise can only help.
lessons.anchor: Turkey's confidence peaks before the end; the barbell of Treasury bills and small speculative bets.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A graphic designer keeps a steady part-time job that covers rent and spends two evenings a week on her own illustration books, where one surprise hit could matter and a flop costs little.

reflect_final: Where in your life does a long calm stretch make you feel safest, and what would day one thousand and one look like there?

use_cases.situation: Your team points to years of stable sales as proof nothing will change.
use_cases.move: Mention Taleb's turkey, whose confidence was highest just before Thanksgiving, and ask what would hurt most if the trend broke.

use_cases.situation: A friend is putting all their savings into one 'moderately risky' plan.
use_cases.move: Describe Taleb's barbell: keep most of it very safe and only a small part in bold bets.

use_cases.situation: You depend on one client or one income source.
use_cases.move: Write down what you would do if it stopped next month, and take one step toward a safety floor.

pocket_idea: The turkey felt safest the day before Thanksgiving; build a floor that a surprise cannot break.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Taleb's turkey grows more confident with every meal for a thousand days, then meets the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Turkey fed daily, confidence peaks, killed before Thanksgiving; Taleb's barbell: very safe floor plus small bold bets.
